title: Fante Fante
author: Naa Oyoo Quartey
desc: The tilapia is steamed dry in its own juices for ten minutes and only then joins the sauce — so it holds together instead of breaking up.
longDesc: Fante fante is the fresh fish stew of the Fante coast, from Cape Coast and Elmina, and the technique that makes it work is cooking the fish separately. Whole tilapia in large chunks is marinated in a blend of onion, ginger, garlic and chilli, then steamed in a dry pan over low heat, covered, for ten minutes in its own juices and flipped gently. Meanwhile koobi fries in half a cup of hot palm oil, the blended tomato and remaining chilli paste go in, and it simmers covered ten minutes until reduced. Okra and the fish join for five minutes at the end.
ingredients: 1 whole tilapia, cut into large chunks
equipment: Dry pan, for steaming the fish
steps: Blend half the onion, the ginger, garlic and 4 of the chilli pieces, and marinate the fish in it with salt.
Heat the palm oil and fry the koobi.
Blend the tomatoes with the remaining onion and chilli paste and add to the pan.
Cover and simmer 10 minutes, until reduced.
Meanwhile steam the tilapia in a dry pan over low heat, covered, 10 minutes in its own juices. Flip gently.
Slice the okra and the remaining chilli into the sauce.
Add the tilapia and cook 5 minutes.
chefTips: Steam the fish dry and separately. A dry pan, low heat, lid on, ten minutes in its own juices — it firms up enough to survive going into the sauce.
Flip gently, once. Tilapia chunks fall apart if turned more than that.
Seven green chillies for two servings is a lot, and they are split — four into the marinade, the rest into the sauce. Green chilli rather than scotch bonnet gives a grassier heat.
Fry the koobi in the palm oil before the tomatoes. Salted fish in hot oil is the flavour base of the whole stew.
Until reduced is the sauce cue at ten minutes covered. It should be thick enough to coat the fish rather than swim it.
Four okra fingers go in near the end with the last chilli. They thicken slightly and add their own texture without taking over.
Soak and clean the koobi first. It is heavily salted and will otherwise make the whole stew inedible.
commonMistakes: Cooking the tilapia in the sauce from raw, so it disintegrates.
Turning the fish repeatedly while it steams.
All seven chillies into the marinade.
Adding the okra at the start, so it collapses.
sources: Adapted from 'Fante Fante Recipe', accramommy.com, 11 January 2024. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Naa Oyoo Quartey'. Yield as printed: serves 2 adults; prep 10, cook 30. The page's cultural note states the dish 'originating from the Fante people' of Cape Coast and Elmina — the basis for the community attribution.

Ingredients exactly as printed: 5 fresh tomatoes, roughly chopped; 1 whole white onion; 7 large green chilli peppers; 2 large ginger pieces; 1 koobi (salted fish), soaked and cleaned; 1 whole tilapia, cut into large chunks; 4 garlic cloves; 4 okra fingers; Salt to taste; ½ cup palm oil.

Method as printed: marinate the fish with half the onion, ginger, garlic and '4 chilli pieces' blended, plus salt; fry the koobi in hot palm oil, add the blended tomato and onion and remaining chilli paste, then cover and simmer 10 minutes 'until reduced'; steam the tilapia in a dry pan over low heat, covered, '10 minutes in its own juices', flipping gently; slice the okra and remaining chilli into the sauce, add the tilapia, cook 5 minutes.
DONENESS CUES, quoted: 'until reduced' for the sauce; '10 minutes in its own juices' for the fish.

THE DRY-STEAM TECHNIQUE for the fish is the distinguishing feature of this recipe and is documented nowhere else in the Ghanaian fish-stew record. It solves the problem every fish stew has — fish that breaks up — and it is reproduced as a separate step rather than folded into the sauce method.
'2 large ginger pieces' is not a quantity and has not been converted.

BYLINE NOTE: this is the same cook whose blog appears elsewhere in this collection under a site-name byline — 'By Naaoyooquartey.com' on a modernghana.com ebunuebunu recipe (see the sources at GHA022). Here her personal byline is printed. The inconsistency is in the publishing, not the authorship, and is recorded.

A CAVEAT ON ATTRIBUTION: the author is not herself described anywhere as Fante. The Fante attribution is her page's claim about the dish's origin, not a claim about her own background, and is recorded on that basis.

THE WIDER RECORD IS THIN: Wikipedia's Ghanaian cuisine article notes that 'palm oil is necessary in okro stew, eto, or fante fante', but NO OTHER NAMED SOURCE for fante fante was found. This is the only quantified recipe for the dish in the material consulted.

A SOURCE REJECTED: theafricangourmet.com has a 'Fetu Afahye' page touching on fante fante, with no byline and a spice list of cumin, coriander, turmeric, paprika and chili with a cilantro garnish. That is a generic profile rather than a Fante recipe and it was not used.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. Fresh fish stew does not keep well.
reheating: Gentle heat, briefly. The fish will break up if stirred.
healthBenefits: Tilapia is lean, high in protein and low in mercury.
Okra contributes soluble fibre, folate and vitamin K.
Red palm oil supplies provitamin-A carotenoids.
Green chillies are high in vitamin C.
culturalNote: Cape Coast and Elmina are fishing towns and fante fante is what you eat there when the catch comes in — the whole dish is built around not ruining a fresh fish. That it is named simply for the people who make it suggests how central it is to them.
